intro: In August 1914 a soldier marched off to war with a rifle, a horse-drawn wagon behind him and a letter home that would take a week to arrive. His great-granddaughter carries in her pocket a device that can reach any person on Earth in a second, and she lives in a world with about eight billion people, nearly two hundred countries, and enough nuclear weapons to end civilization in an afternoon. Between those two lives lie two world wars that killed tens of millions, the rise and fall of dictatorships that claimed the right to control every thought, a forty-year standoff between two superpowers, the end of the European empires, and the wiring together of the whole planet. This unit covers that century.

The three chapters follow a shape. The first, from 1914 to 1945, shows how modern states learned to organize whole societies for war and, in the worst cases, for murder, and how the world tried twice to build something to stop it happening again. The second, from 1945 to 1991, follows a divided world in which the superpowers never fought each other directly but fought through Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and dozens of other places, while more than half of humanity, in India, Africa, Asia and the Middle East, won independence from empires. The third, from 1991 to today, is about the world those endings made: one connected economy, a rising China, wars that began on a single morning in 2001, and problems such as climate, disease, migration and inequality that no border can hold back.

You will read the evidence: a soldier's letter from a Christmas truce, a president's words after Pearl Harbor, the Nazis' own train schedules, a leader's statement from the dock at his trial, a curve of carbon dioxide measured on a Hawaiian volcano. You will meet people who held total power and people who stood in front of tanks, and you will see how the same event can carry two names for two peoples. By the end you should be able to explain how the twentieth century made the world you live in, to argue with evidence about who gained and who paid, and to bring a historian's habits to the flood of news that reaches your own screen every day.
bigQuestion: From 1914 to today, what did people learn, and fail to learn, about how much power a government should hold over its own people and over the world?

timeline.t: An assassination in Sarajevo pulls Europe's alliances into a world war; soldiers hold a Christmas truce
The United States enters the war; Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power in Russia in November
The Treaty of Versailles punishes Germany and creates a League of Nations the United States never joins
The Great Depression spreads around the world; Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany in 1933
World War II; the Holocaust murders six million Jews; atomic bombs destroy Hiroshima and Nagasaki
The United Nations is founded; the iron curtain divides Europe; NATO forms and Mao wins China
India and Pakistan become independent at midnight; partition uproots some fifteen million people
Ghana leads Africa toward independence; the Cuban Missile Crisis brings the world to the edge
American troops fight in Vietnam until the last leave in 1973 and Saigon falls in 1975
The Berlin Wall opens; the Soviet Union dissolves on Christmas Day 1991
Mandela is elected in South Africa; the World Wide Web spreads; the attacks of September 11
The Paris climate agreement; a million refugees reach Europe; COVID-19 becomes a pandemic

words.d: a war in which a nation's whole economy and population are organized to support the fighting
describing a state that tries to control every part of public and private life
giving a hostile power what it demands in the hope of avoiding war
the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
a country whose military and economic strength far exceed all others, as the United States and Soviet Union after 1945
the American policy of stopping communism from spreading beyond where it already held power
the idea that a nuclear attack by either side would destroy both, so neither dares strike
the process by which colonies became independent countries, mostly between 1945 and 1975
South Africa's legal system of racial separation and white rule from 1948 to 1994
the growing connection of the world's economies and cultures through trade, travel, money and information
a person who has fled his or her country because of war or persecution and cannot safely return
false information spread deliberately to deceive

test.q: Why did a killing in Sarajevo in 1914 become a war among all the great powers within five weeks?
choices: Because Serbia invaded Germany
Because the alliance system pulled each power in as its partner was threatened, and war plans left no time to talk
Because the League of Nations ordered it
Because Britain wanted Austria's colonies
test.why: Germany backed Austria, Russia backed Serbia, France and Britain were tied to Russia, and mobilization plans made each step trigger the next.

test.q: What did the machine gun, artillery and barbed wire do to warfare on the Western Front?
choices: They made cavalry charges more effective
They ended the war within months
They made attacking across open ground so deadly that both sides dug trenches and the front barely moved for years
They were banned by both sides after 1915
test.why: Defense became far stronger than attack, so battles like the Somme cost enormous casualties for a few miles of ground.

test.q: Which promise won Lenin's Bolsheviks support among soldiers, peasants and workers in 1917?
choices: Victory over Germany
A restored tsar
Free elections within a year
Peace, land and bread
test.why: Each word spoke to a group the temporary government had failed: war-weary soldiers, land-hungry peasants and hungry city workers.

test.q: How did the Great Depression help bring Hitler to power?
choices: Mass unemployment after 1929 turned the Nazis from a fringe party into Germany's largest party by 1932
It made Germany rich enough to rearm
It ended the Treaty of Versailles
It caused Britain to support the Nazis
test.why: With roughly a third of the workforce jobless, voters turned to a party promising order and greatness, and Hindenburg appointed Hitler in 1933.

test.q: What do the Nazi and Stalinist states have in common that makes historians call both totalitarian?
choices: Both were monarchies
Both held free elections
Both tried to control every part of life and used terror against their own people
Both were created by the League of Nations
test.why: Their ideas were opposites, but their methods, total control backed by secret police, camps and propaganda, were much the same.

test.q: What pattern do the events from Manchuria in 1931 to Munich in 1938 show?
choices: Aggressors were stopped quickly by the League
Each time an aggressor got away with a seizure, the next demand was larger
The democracies attacked first
The Soviet Union defended every victim
test.why: Japan, Italy and Germany each took territory without being stopped, and appeasement at Munich was followed within months by the seizure of Czechoslovakia.

test.q: What kinds of evidence establish what happened in the Holocaust?
choices: Only rumors passed among soldiers
The Nazis' own records, Allied photographs and films of the camps, and survivor testimony
Novels written after the war
Guesses made by historians in the 1980s
test.why: Train schedules, camp registers and killing-squad reports, together with liberation footage and testimony at Nuremberg and since, document the planned murder of about six million Jews.

test.q: Why was the conflict between the superpowers after 1947 called a Cold War?
choices: It was fought only in winter
Neither side had nuclear weapons
It was fought entirely at sea
The United States and the Soviet Union competed for decades but never fought each other directly
test.why: The rivalry was fought with money, weapons, propaganda and other people's wars, such as Korea and Vietnam, rather than by direct battle.

test.q: What lesson did Kennedy and Khrushchev take from the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962?
choices: That an enemy in a nuclear world needs a way out, which led to the hotline and a test ban treaty
That Cuba should be invaded
That air strikes always work
That treaties are useless
test.why: Each leader chose an exit that let the other save face, and both sides then began talking to make the rivalry less dangerous.

test.q: What did the American war in Vietnam and the Soviet war in Afghanistan have in common?
choices: Both ended with a superpower victory
Both were fought against France
A superpower with overwhelming firepower could not defeat local guerrillas and withdrew after heavy losses
Both lasted less than two years
test.why: In each war a superpower backed a weak government against guerrillas armed by its rival, and firepower could win battles but not the war.

test.q: What did Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 demonstrate?
choices: That India needed a larger army
That breaking an unjust law openly and accepting punishment without violence could shake an empire
That Britain would never leave India
That partition was the only answer
test.why: Gandhi's satyagraha turned a small act, picking up salt, into a challenge the empire could not answer without looking unjust before the world.

test.q: Which problem did most new African states inherit from colonial rule?
choices: Too many trained doctors and administrators
Membership in the Warsaw Pact
A lack of any natural resources
Borders drawn in Europe that cut across peoples, and economies built to export one or two raw materials
test.why: The flags changed in the 1950s and 1960s, but the borders of the 1880s and export economies priced abroad remained, as the Congo's collapse showed.

test.q: Why does the year 1948 carry two opposite names, the War of Independence and the Nakba?
choices: Because Israel and Egypt signed a peace treaty that year
Because the same events gave Jews a state after the Holocaust and drove about seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs from their homes
Because the United Nations refused to divide Palestine
Because the oil embargo began that year
test.why: Both memories describe real events: a state founded three years after the death camps and a people who locked their doors and never returned.

test.q: What single change made the peaceful revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe possible?
choices: Gorbachev's decision that the Soviet army would no longer save those governments from their own people
A NATO invasion
China's support for reform
A United Nations resolution
test.why: Without the threat of Soviet tanks, governments that had ruled by fear faced crowds in Leipzig, Prague and Berlin alone, and most would not order a massacre.

test.q: Which statement about globalization since 1991 does the unit support?
choices: Every person and place gained equally
No one gained at all
Only rich countries gained
The world as a whole grew richer and less poor while losses fell hard on particular places, such as factory towns in Illinois
test.why: Extreme poverty fell from about one in three people to under one in ten, while towns like Galesburg lost their largest employers and never fully recovered.

write.prompt: Make a claim: between 1914 and today, did the world learn how to limit what governments can do to people, or did it mostly fail? Support your claim with evidence from at least two chapters of this unit and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence, and say what you mean by learn: new rules, new institutions, or changed behavior.
Use specific evidence: the League and the United Nations, the Nuremberg trials and the Genocide Convention, Rwanda in 1994, the Cuban Missile Crisis, 1989, the International Criminal Court.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence supports your claim rather than just listing events.
Take the other side seriously: what would someone who disagrees point to, and why does your evidence outweigh it?
Give dates and eras for every person and event you use, and say how we know what happened.
